I didn't know that. I know (unintelligible). Well, you see, the lady with the first vocalist (inaudible).
How did you come to (inaudible)? She was with you (inaudible)?

Yeah. [I met her] (Inaudible) through John Hammond, you know, and she was singing at Monroe's Place uptown. That's where I first heard her. She was (inaudible) teens then. Really, (inaudible). John took her by and listened to her. She had really a strange way of delivering a song, you know? All so wonderful. (Inaudible) with the band.

Yes. It was such a beautiful idea, too, you know, and it really caught on with him. John said, 'You should listen to this girl sing because I think she would fit your band.' I heard her and that was it.
You remember what she was singing that night?
Do you remember what she was singing that night, the night you heard her?
No. No, I don't. I just remembered it just (inaudible) Billie Holiday, just (inaudible) remember Billie.
Did she come over to talk to you at all?
Not really, (inaudible). John introduced me and all and we talked just a little bit, not too much.
But -- so he took care of it. He said, you know --
Yeah, well, I mean, (inaudible) -- it didn't happen just right away, you know.
Not just right like the next week or something like that, you know.
It was just a little while later. And I guess Billie's (inaudible) with her mother (inaudible) still a very young girl.
That would be in '37? She would be -- well, in '37, she would have been 22.
--22? You think she was younger even than (inaudible) teenager?
How was that year, her being with the band? How did she change things for the band? Did she have any kind of effect in that way?
Why, I don't -- how do you mean?
He was singing? Oh, he was along with you. He was singing during that time, too, wasn't he?
But a girl vocalist (inaudible). He hadn't had a girl vocalist.
Did she make any change in the girl vocalists, girl singing?
-- change really. You mean in how --
Yeah, attitude, in terms of musically or --

Oh, I don't know. Oh, I think musically, I think it was a great change, greatest (inaudible). Great change, something added that just was a -- that it was a wonderful attraction (inaudible). Everybody loved her. Everybody got along well with her. She got along well with all the guys and this was something else which was great. And as far as I'm concerned, I mean, I'd look for the night (inaudible) go to work to hear her sing. She just killed me.
Do you have any favorite? Did you at that time (inaudible)?
Yeah. Two songs she used to sing, I'd cry for either of them. (Inaudible).
No, every time we got a little thing (inaudible).
Yeah. Would it be you and she or the whole band?
Yeah? How much room was there for, you know, these were head arrangements or --
No, no. We had arrangements for her, sure.
How much would they (inaudible) change though, in terms of -- she would sing differently every night. You sing every song differently (inaudible)?
I mean, she would sing a song different, the same song different each time she sang it.

Oh, I don't know. Well, that I never paid any attention to that. I mean, it's, you know, it's -- (inaudible) I don't really think (inaudible). She just sang it wonderfully every night. I don't know whether it changes or not, how -- whether she sang it differently or not, I mean, she just sang good every night.
How much improvisation was there in musicians?
I don't know. What would you say?

What would you say? I guess it would depend on the musician. I guess that's what I'd say. I mean, there are musicians I could hear how they (inaudible) changes. I mean, some might -- I just know would play the same thing. Would you say that's true, depending on --
And depending on the musician, I guess.
Jo Jones said that -- he said that John Hammond fired Billie because she wouldn't sing the blues.

No, that isn't so. (inaudible) Billie sang the blues at times. I mean, little Billie, I think Billie (inaudible) sing the blues. Couple things she sang the blues in her way. Billie wasn't a blues singer.
I don't think. But she had a blues a thing she used to sing, but she wasn't a blues singer, no. She was -- she's a stylist, (inaudible) stylist, you know. She
She -- whatever (inaudible), whatever (inaudible). I don't even touch that.
But did you know her to refuse to sing the blues exclusively? I mean, did --
I knew her could sing blues exclusively.
She sang very few blues, right?
I mean, (inaudible) think of three. Somehow, you know, blues (inaudible) --
Yeah, well, see, she wasn't a blues singer (inaudible).
Well, why would Jo Jones be saying this? I mean, he's really, you know, he's told a number of people -- I just, you know, didn't know if it were true or not or if --
Was it true what she said in her book about having to wear dark make-up in Detroit (inaudible) because she was too light at that time, considered too light for Fox Theater?
There was Fox Theater and there was some (inaudible) with what you say it was or dancers -- there's a whole thing, you know, like Radio City almost, or something.
She said that (inaudible) that you said that she had to darken her face because she was at that time, she was too light to sing with a black band, considered too light?
I don't know. Maybe it happened.
I just heard her sing. She (inaudible) I didn't know anything about, see?
Did you travel -- did you all stay together at the same place?
Yeah, most of the time we did.
Yeah. That's why they had so much fun.
(Inaudible), you know. Everybody was together. We'd have a little taste, you know what I mean? Just the gang together.
Did you ever ride with her (inaudible)?
I never sit with her, no. She had a seat by herself.
Do you feel it was tough for her as a girl, to be, you know, --
No tougher than it is now. I -- what I think -- I think maybe black people are tougher now than was then.

Well, I don't know. See, might be tough for a girl now, because maybe the girls now -- maybe they weren't like Billie. I mean, maybe the guys aren't like the guys then. I mean, you see, Billie was just the same, remember, really, a musician, you know?
The guys -- that's the way the guys felt about Billie, you know? I mean, the guys really felt like they were all -- were -- could get in the bus and relax, you know
what I mean? They wouldn't have to watch -- say, "Watch out, brother," you know what I mean? But anybody else got in the bus would have to watch it.
You know? Anybody else that wasn't in the family would have to watch it, cool it. You know, it's -- we were all together.
Did you have any special things going? In the family? I mean, you know, things that were special, you know, like sometimes things develop among people (inaudible) either lines or words, you know --
Of course, she and Prez (PHONETIC) had things going. I mean, they invent a lot of things -- Prez invented the language he had with her.
And as a matter of fact, I think Prez named her.
Yeah. They used to have little things going on and they were something.
He had a lot of little (inaudible). He invented a lot of things, Prez.
Do you remember any of them?
No, (inaudible). Old Prez character everybody remembers a few of his (inaudible) last days. I mean, (inaudible) little sayings that can't remember any of them now, he used to say, but I (inaudible).
What did he used to call you?
What did Billie used to call you?
(Inaudible) I don't think Billie had a name for me.
I don't think Billie had a name for me.
Did she call you Bill? Count?
She used to call you Daddy Basie?
She had a way, didn't she?
Like I was watching the -- you know that TV program that you did, 'The Sound of Jazz?'
And I remember when you were playing something and she came out, you know, it was all very casual, and she just kind of talking to you and there just seemed to be something so tight, you know?

(Inaudible) tight (inaudible). Much tighter, much tighter, tighter than that. (Inaudible) I loved Billie as far as that kind of love can go. I have to get some water (inaudible). I loved Billie an awful lot.
When you played for her, did you play differently?
When you played for her, did you play differently -- played with her, did you play differently? In any way that you (inaudible) were aware of?

No, I -- no, no. We (inaudible) play any different for her than we would play for any other singer. (Inaudible) because any singer that sings good, you play, you play the best you can, you know, but you just feel differently, you know, within yourself, you know?
That's right. (Inaudible). Now you're saying something.
How did you feel different? Playing for her?
Now, you see, then I wouldn't know it because that was the first woman (inaudible) playing for, you know? And -- oh, I don't know. Playing for her, playing for her, that was just too wonderful.
I'm not going to let you have that (inaudible). I wish you could have it, but I'm not going to let you have it.
Oh, the story. No, I wanted to run it for a reason. I don't need a story. I mean, I wanted to run what you were talking about, just --
Hm? I can get anything (inaudible). No, I was -- the reason I was turning this on --
You got some strange things happening here.
Well, I mean, maybe we could go to another --
It's not (inaudible) questions that I have, I'd just really like to know, is -- what it was like?
No, I know they're not questions, darling, they're just lead-ons or something.

Lead-ons. Well, what I really would like to hear is tell me about that year that you were all on the road, you know? Tell me about, you know, focusing on (inaudible), whatever comes into your mind. What were the things that happened or the, you know --
Well, do you know one thing? Do you know one thing? In her book, she put in there, put damn near had everything in there, what happened on the road.
Like what? What'd she have on there that
happened with us on the road? You see, I mean, there were really no outstanding -- Incidents?
Right, that really actually happened which you would just get into.
You know? Average travel, like we were, and--
Where do you feel you were, in terms of your career?
Where do you feel you were, in terms of your career?
Where do I feel that I were?
Where were you then, that year, in terms of --
Yeah, that year. I mean, you were just starting out. What were the things that were difficult in getting together, you know, getting your sound together, everything together?
Well, not really now. Come to think of it, what was the tough things?
Come to think of it, what was the tough things? Now, that is something that is a question. You're phenomenal. You are --
-- tough things. Well, it really wasn't tough.
Because we worked, we were working.

And that's all you wanted to do, was to work, and we had a fairly nice band. We were working hard with the band together, you know, and we were happy together. Then when Lady Day joined us, I mean, that we -- then we were a very happy group. We just -- well, it was happy all the time. Now,
you say, now, unhappy? The rough times? Now, I guess we could say -- and you're doing your one-nighters, I guess we'll say, maybe we'll say your living conditions possibly.
We had to do maybe some parts of the United States where it was sort of rough.
Now, it seems like it was rough then. But even so, we're having a lot of fun then because we were younger then. I mean, you could figure out, I mean, then you were 25 or 30 years younger then --
Uh-huh, so you could take it.
You could take it, it's no mind. I mean, and that's from year to year, going to places like this, it got to be, you'd say you'd look forward to --
This type things, you know? You get used to it.
And those conditions that you were really used to. And we were all trying to really actually trying to find out, asking myself, why was it so tough?
I wonder why. Come to think of it, it wasn't so rough after all.
Wait until I bring that question up now, to really --

Wait until I get some of the old guys together again and we get around, sit around and get in a conversation. I'll bring this up. Say, "You know, it really wasn't that rough years ago. (Inaudible) it wasn't." Because we were working, really working and getting paid for working.

Well, it would be like -- (inaudible) if you was with a show and you was getting paid with a meal ticket, something like that, you know, I mean, during the (inaudible) get any money or anything like that [now].
You didn't make any bread each night?
No, you just, you worked and you got a meal ticket, you know, (inaudible) played all them shows, you know, things like that.
And you would get enough to cover expenses?
They'd pay you -- the show would pick it up. Nobody like that in our band, they know -- they didn't know
anything about anything (inaudible) the kids were too young for that.
(Inaudible) on one of those kind of things, you know? I think maybe the old veterans, you know, those kind of things --
Billie said that she played -- that she was making 125 bucks a week.
Well, she was making more money than anybody else.
Well, I guess she was. Yeah, I guess she was.
Could she have been making that much money?
If she says she was making $125 per week, that's what she was making.
She may not have said it though. The person who wrote the book might have said it.
Well, did you say that Billie said she made it?
Well, I mean, it's a question of whether, you know --
-- who wrote the book, you know.
-- contradict Billie. Well, I'm not going to contradict Billie at all. So, let's go to some other question.
Okay. What were the instruments like? Like when you -- what kind of pianos did you have to play on?
Same kind of pianos now almost, sometimes. Sometimes, good ones. Sometimes, bad ones. Sometimes, very bad ones. Same thing happens right now.
Sometimes, very bad ones. Pianos haven't changed.
What kind of places were you playing that year?
And you say that the band was fairly good. Why only fairly good?
Well, we were trying, darling. We were trying, (inaudible) --
Well, we were trying -- I say that. I always say that with any band I have.
But you've never heard me say a band's great, do you?
Yeah. Did you ever feel you did have a great band?
I feel I always have a fairly nice band.
Have you ever felt that you're going --
I just feel like I had a fairly nice band. Don't take me any further than that, please.
Okay. In thinking back to that band, the musicians you had together, when (inaudible), how would that band differ from the other bands you had?
I thought we were talking about Billie Holiday.
Well, what are we talking about bands for?
Well, it was your band she was singing with.
Are we still talking about Billie Holiday?
Well, you interviewing me about my band or Billie Holiday?
Both. I can't write about Billie Holiday with your band, if I'm not going to talk about your band.
You say how did the band differ from any other band?
Yeah, how was that band (inaudible)? I mean, the organization, you know, the people, part of it, the spirit, everything.
I don't know what was special about it.
I don't think so. I just think that maybe the style of the band was different than anybody else's. But whether it was better than anybody else's band, the style
was different possibly. I never said it was better than anybody else's band.
Oh, I didn't say it was.
Yeah. How did you feel the style was different?
Well, I don't know. Just different, I guess. I imagine the style was different.
Did you and Billie have any --
Because we didn't. We didn't never really joke. (Inaudible) good thing.
What kind of communication did you have?
Well, I don't know. I don't know what's -- we would have a little taste maybe and then maybe like

if we'd get into a town early or play a Heater or something like that, or something like that, we'd go with Billie. All the guys, usually the guys that Billie liked that were real close to Billie, I mean, you'd go up to Billie's for -- probably go to Billie's room and Billie had a nice record player. We'd listen to records, you know, (inaudible).
What record did you listen to? What records would you listen to?
Do you remember that? Do you remember that?
You remember the night you did that or do you remember the Savoy?
What do you remember about it?
I remember what a beautiful engagement that was.

It was just so beautiful because it was a gorgeous engagement; the kids up there just loved her, you know? And it's a strange thing, it was almost a -- Ella was on one stand and we was on Chick, you know, Chick Webb. (Inaudible) the other. I mean, (inaudible) But and then we played the Apollo Theater. That's what really -- that's really where she really did shine. I never would forget that. That was beautiful (inaudible). I mean, she just couldn't get off the stage there. The last date I played with William, I (inaudible) hospital (inaudible). She was so (inaudible) and that was Sammy Davis for Broadway.
Getting off the point right there, too, also. (Inaudible). Yep, (inaudible).
Because Sammy used to introduce her.
He used to. Is that point in the show?
Yeah, yeah. Sammy was just beginning to -- that was just the getting off point then for that -- for the Will Mastin (Unaudible) Trio, getting right there that week.
What did you think of Sammy Davis that show, that --

Geez, I'd never seen anything like it. I first saw him down in -- first time I saw him was down in Memphis and I never seen anything like it, like him. And I just knew I had to see him. I knew he had to be with me. It was grand.
That's right. There's no greater talent in the world than this kid.

Yeah, I have some questions, I just remembered. Do you remember that -- oh, no -- yeah, right. You know, the midnight jazz concert in 1948, right after -- that was right after they came out -- all this -- right, because she came out in March. And you did this midnight jazz concert for the Pittsburgh Courier. I think Sarah Vaughan was on it. I think --
Oh, yeah, wait. In 1954, you did Birdland Stars of '54 Concert, two concerts at Carnegie, 8:30 and
midnight, with Sarah and Billie. Uh-huh. You don't remember the two of them together?
Well, how about at this Savoy, when Chick Webb and Ella were, you know, opposite here and Billie? What do you remember about that? Why was that so exciting?
It was a beautiful night, because I think that was the first night Billie worked at Savoy.
Uh-huh. What was beautiful about it, aside from the fact that it was her first night?
Well, what was beautiful about it?
I think, well, because everybody loved it, it was so wonderful and Billie was so great there. It was great.
Well, I mean, how was it -- like opposite Chick and Ella?
How was it like that, opposite them?
Opposite, yeah, did that create excitement?
Oh, it was no battle. It wasn't any battle or thing like that.
No, it was no contest or anything like
that, but we were just up there for that one night and -- I think.
Yeah. Wait a second. No, you had a long engagement at the Savoy.
I think it might have been a week or two even.
Was it a week? Was it?
I'm not sure though. I'm not sure.
Well, then, they must have came in for one night or something like that. I don't know which one -- one of the two (inaudible).
Yeah. But I mean, did that kind of like spur you on, you know? Was it exciting to play opposite them?
Oh, yes, it's very exciting to play opposite them, because --
What does it do to you?
I want you to just know this much, I mean, that you know, with the First Lady of Swing up there, and Chick Webb and that band he had --
Did you ever hear that band?
Uh-huh -- no, I never did. I mean, not in person.
(Inaudible) if you had an orchestra, (inaudible), you didn't want to get mixed up with them.
Because he had a bad one, boy.
Yeah, he was a bad motorcycle hisself.
What was the difference between what Ella did that night and what Lady did that night?
Two different styles. Now, you're no Indian now. You keep on saying 'how.'
She said that she was making $14 a day. That's what she said.
How much does that come to a week?
I got (inaudible). Anyway, yeah, well, you're not going to --
I mean, you know, the lady said, so I might as well just ask you anyway.

Because she said that Jimmy Rushing never lent anybody any money. She was very angry at him once because she and Prez needed some bread and Jimmy said, 'No, save your pennies,' and that he was like that.
Well, I don't know about that.
Kind of put her down. I just wanted to (inaudible).
I don't know. How do I know?
Did you ever see her shoot crap in a bus?
Did you ever see her shoot crap in a bus?
How was she? Was she good?
Who used to win most of the bread in craps? Who was the best?
I don't know. Don't look at me. It wasn't me.
You used to shoot with her?
Well, you ain't going to let her action go off without me getting in it, do you?
Did she lend musicians money? Did she have any to lend?
Did she have any money to lend at all? you could get
She said you weren't your own boss, that you had too many managers.
Herschel Evans, did he resent Lester because Billie wanted him to play behind her?
Well, miss, I don't know. I think (inaudible) they has something going there.
All right, forget Freddie Green, right?
I'm not going to tell you.
No, no, she was always real good on Freddie Green.
Who, she? Oh, she just said she just loved him.
You ain't going to tell -- you see?
You see, you ain't going to let it hang out. You say you want me to tell it.
I ain't going to tell you nothing else.
Did you play a lot of riffraff during
I don't know what they are.
Well, I don't call no place a riffraff that pays me.
Ah, very well said, very well said.
She said that you used to alternate riffraff joints and then you'd play some good white hotel and that you'd go from one extreme to the other. Is that true?
Okay. You didn't have the right uniforms, clothes or equipment.
The band didn't have the right uniforms or clothes or equipment.
What would we work in, overalls?
How about the horns? Did you ever see -- did Prez's horn have rubber bands?
Yeah, was that part of the problem at the beginning? I mean, when you say --
Let me tell you something. They use rubber bands now, sweetheart.
Yeah, why do they use them?

Sometimes, I mean, the spring breaks (inaudible) times on their horns and they use them until they can get springs to replace them, until they can get to someplace where they can fix them, find some springs.
Who did Billie like to play behind her on trumpet?
Oh, Clayton usually, in the band.
Now, what would I know? I mean --
What was the difference between Buck and Sweets' sound? Playing behind Billie?
Let me ask you this. That's not a very bright question. Let me ask you this. Let me change it. That was a dumb question. What I really, I think, what I
really mean is when would Buck play and when would Sweets play? Did it ever form a pattern?
When did they have to form a pattern?
I mean, did it ever form a pattern, when they played behind? How much of this would be planned?
How much of it would be in the arrangement and how much of it would just come up spontaneously?
Well, none of it would be an arrangement.
How much room was there for that?
Well, I don't know. They'd find a space.
But did you ever feel that they felt out the same places, that Sweets had his place that he felt out and that Buck had his place?
That's the way it always would be. That's the only way it could be done.
What was Sweets' place and what was Buck's place? Did it ever, you know, did they ever -- could you always say, 'Now, Buck is going to come in here,' you felt that he was?
--A good question for me to ask you? what would be
That's another question. That's another dumb one.
What would be a good question for you to ask me?
About Billie, yes. What would be a good question?
Ain't that a hell of a thing for you to say.
What would there be a good question for you to ask me.
If it -- if I would ask you that, I'd just want to talk about --
I'd just wait on and just start talking. wade You wouldn't have to ask me no questions.
Ask me a question about Billie.
Me ask you a question about Billie?
: Go ahead. You ask me. What would you ask somebody about --
What would I ask you about Billie?
: Yeah. What would you ask anybody who knew Billie, not me.
That knew her? Well, I tell you what I'd ask you.
What do you really think that Billie thought about life?
: What do you think Billie thought about life? It's a good question. Well, answer it.
Because you want me to answer that question.
Why do you want me to answer that question?
I don't think she liked to be alone. I don't think she could be alone.
-- think Billie liked to be alone.
You don't? She always needed people around, didn't she?
Oh, she could be, I guess.
What did she think? What was her philosophy of life? You asked me that question.
Then why did she have to stay high all the time? I mean --
Why did she always need drugs?
Why did she always need drugs?
In such excess, yes, if she loved life that much.
Well, do you know what happened? That could have been a very unfortunate thing.
I don't think it started that way. I think that really got out of hand. I just think that's something that was just done and just couldn't stop and then after this appears in this way --
-- then that [challenge] just had to have it.
This (inaudible) was coming to take care of (inaudible).
Was she on any hard stuff, the year she was (inaudible) on the band?
I don't know when this started -- all this started, oh, God, so much longer after that, you see, (inaudible) because, I mean, (inaudible).
Did you ever belong to that Viper Society, I mean, was there a part for you in those towns when you were out?
Was there a part for you, you know, the Viper Society?
No, very few people I've ever known (inaudible) do anything.
Ever seen them -- see me do anything.
Just you looked like that she was me?
Looked like she was my sweetie?
Well, what are you talking about?
What did you like about her?
I mean, there are a couple of things I couldn't tell you.
Well, tell one of the things you could.
Is there anything you could tell me?
Yes, I could tell you -- I could tell you -- oh, what could I say?
about something. She'd make me -- used to try to make me angry or something would happen, what would happen, she'd do something, deliberately do something.
You mean, she'd try to arouse you?
What would she do? She'd do something silly.

Always doing her Always singing Boys don't want a job. (Unintelligible). always straight on the job, And (unintelligible) you know? You know what I mean? Never juiced or to never -- out of her mind, you know?
You mean never during that year or never thereafter? All the times you were together?
That's right. All these other things you're talking about, that's really Johnny-come-lately, which I don't know. I don't think she knew what was happening, really. (inaudible).
... Lady Day -- I wanted to really be like that.
What do you think she wanted to be like?
Like knowing nothing about any things.
That's right. Do you know anything about any drugs for yourself?
You mean did I ever shoot up?
That meant that I believed (unintelligible) that's the way she really would like to be, to have been.
What was the difference? What was the difference?
What do you mean, what was the difference?
What was the difference then and now?

I don't know, because I only knew her one way. I wasn't around when the other thing happened. [How] ^ The other thing happened, I don't know. People talk about different things. I don't know. I don't know what happened.
I worked with her again at Strayer the Strand (PHONETIC). She was beautiful then, every show.
So I don't know whatever, you know.
So, whatever happened, so I don't know --
What were the things that you were thinking of --
That was the interview with Count
Basie on November 3rd, 1971 at the Penn Harris Hotel in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania.
